Just a few days of dangerous heat each year may be linked to greater dementia risk, according to a 20-year US study that reveals how neighborhood disadvantage and limited cooling infrastructure could leave some communities more vulnerable.
Study: Outdoor extreme heat-related dementia risk and the role of socioeconomic disparities: evidence from 20 years of data on US older adults. Image credit: Rainer Fuhrmann/Shutterstock.com
Exposure to just a few days of extreme outdoor heat each year may be linked to a higher risk of dementia, according to a study of more than 28,000 US adults using data spanning two decades, published in the journal Alzheimer’s & Dementia. The findings suggest that socially vulnerable communities with limited cooling infrastructure may face greater risks.
Extreme heat raises concerns about long-term dementia risk
Extreme heat poses significant health risks, particularly for older adults, who are more vulnerable to its effects. Previous studies have linked hot weather to poorer cognitive performance and faster cognitive decline, while growing evidence suggests that socioeconomic disadvantage may further increase vulnerability. People with fewer financial resources may have limited access to healthcare and cooling facilities, greater exposure to outdoor heat, and less social support during heat-related illness.
Housing conditions can also influence heat exposure. Older, poorly insulated homes and mobile homes may retain more heat, while rural communities may face additional challenges because of aging housing, limited healthcare access, and lower air-conditioning (AC) use.
Despite these concerns, little is known about whether prolonged exposure to extreme outdoor heat is associated with the development of dementia in the general older population. Two previous studies from Taiwan examined dementia risk among people with a history of heat-related illness, but their findings may not apply to the broader population.
To address this gap, the researchers investigated whether cumulative outdoor heat exposure was associated with new-onset dementia in a nationally representative US cohort and whether socioeconomic circumstances and neighborhood conditions influenced this association.
Twenty years of data reveal heat exposure patterns
The study drew on data obtained from 2000 to 2020 from the Health and Retirement Study (HRS). It included 28,512 community-dwelling, dementia-free adults aged 50 to 89 at baseline, with an average starting age of 59.8 years, with at least one follow-up over an average of 10.5 years. During that time, 3,773 developed dementia (13.2%) and 7,887 died without a dementia classification (27.7%).
Dementia was identified using the validated Langa–Weir algorithm, based on cognitive assessments and proxy reports. To reduce false positives, researchers generally required an initial dementia classification to be followed by another assessment indicating dementia or cognitive impairment. Participants classified with dementia who died before the next survey wave were also counted as cases.
Heat exposure was categorized by the daily heat index (which combines air temperature and humidity to estimate how hot conditions feel), which was estimated for each respondent's census tract from 4-km gridMET data. Days were classified into two National Weather Service categories: Extreme Caution, at 90–102°F (32.2–39.3°C), and Danger+ at 103°F (39.4°C) or higher. Across the study observations, participants experienced an average of 5.8 Danger+ heat days per year.
To obtain the exposure window, heat days were counted over the preceding five years and recalculated at each wave. The researchers used move dates to map changes in residential location.
The researchers also examined whether personal circumstances and neighborhood conditions influenced the association between extreme heat and dementia. At the individual level, these included markers of socioeconomic deprivation, such as low education, non-housing wealth, living alone, and living in a mobile home. They also attempted to capture differences in neighborhood heat-mitigative resources, such as the Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), tract-level estimated prevalence of central air conditioning (AC), and the degree of urbanization.
They used Fine–Gray weighted subdistribution hazard models to estimate dementia risk, with death as a competing event and age as the time scale. They adjusted for demographics, cardiometabolic conditions, smoking, drinking, region, calendar year, and the effects of the moderating factors.
Dementia associations emerge at the highest heat-index levels
The researchers found no statistically significant association between the number of days of Extreme Caution heat-index conditions and dementia, irrespective of exposure quartile. Conversely, Danger+ heat-index conditions were associated with higher dementia incidence in some exposure categories.
Compared with the lowest exposure (0.2 or fewer Danger+ days per year), moderate exposure (0.4–1.8 days/year) carried a 14% higher subdistribution hazard.
At moderate-high exposure (2–7 days/year), there was no significant increase in risk compared to the lowest exposure. High exposure (7.2 or more days/year) carried a 23% higher hazard.
Thus, the dose-response pattern was not monotonic. However, they found clearly separated cumulative curves for low and high exposure to Danger+ heat, particularly among older people. In contrast, the Extreme Caution curves remained close together. However, these were unadjusted curves.
Neither heat category was significantly associated with mortality in the primary analysis. Therefore, the authors suggest that a five-year cumulative measure captures something different from the acute heat spikes that drive heat-related deaths.
Neighborhood disadvantage strengthens heat-associated dementia risk
The link between extreme heat and dementia was particularly pronounced in disadvantaged neighborhoods, suggesting that where people live may influence their vulnerability to prolonged heat exposure.
Among those experiencing the highest levels of Danger+, the predicted dementia hazard was 40% higher in the most socially vulnerable neighborhoods, compared with 11% higher in less vulnerable areas. Both figures were calculated against the lowest heat-exposure group, with a 26% relative difference between the predicted hazard ratios.
Access to cooling infrastructure also appeared to matter. In neighborhoods with lower estimated central air-conditioning (AC) prevalence, the predicted dementia hazard was 36% higher among those with the greatest heat exposure, compared with 13% higher in areas where central AC was more common. This represented a 20% relative difference between the predicted hazard ratios.
These differences emerged only at the highest levels of dangerous heat. At lower exposure levels, neighborhood vulnerability and AC prevalence did not significantly alter the association with dementia.
Interestingly, individual circumstances, including education, household wealth, living alone, and mobile home residence, did not significantly modify the association. Neither did whether participants lived in urban or less urban areas.
Longer heat exposure windows show more consistent associations
The association between extreme heat and dementia remained largely consistent when researchers tested their findings using different methods, particularly among those with the highest exposure to Danger+ heat (a heat index of 103°F or higher). However, the association at moderate exposure levels was less consistent.
After accounting for residential moves and transitions into nursing homes, the dementia hazard remained 19% higher in the highest Danger+ exposure group, while the association at moderate exposure was no longer statistically significant.
The researchers also examined whether unusually hot conditions relative to each neighborhood's historical climate were associated with dementia. Using this alternative measure, those in the highest exposure group had a 15% higher dementia hazard. The smaller association suggested that the absolute intensity of heat may be more important than how unusual the temperature is for a particular area.
The findings changed little after accounting for air pollution. The length of heat exposure also appeared to matter. When researchers extended the exposure window from five to seven years, the association remained similar, with a 21% higher dementia hazard in the highest exposure group. However, shortening the window to three years reduced the estimate to 12%, which was not statistically significant. This suggests that the association may become more apparent over longer periods, although the study could not establish a cumulative causal effect.
To determine whether the findings were driven by the hotter southern United States, researchers repeated the analysis among 17,298 participants living outside the South. The association persisted, with dementia hazards 26% and 30% higher in the moderate and highest Danger+ exposure groups, respectively, compared with the lowest exposure group.
Finally, the researchers broadened their definition of dementia to include 370 additional participants whose classifications had not remained consistent across assessments. Even with these cases included, the highest Danger+ exposure group had a 19% higher dementia hazard, reinforcing the consistency of the main finding.
Severe heat may trigger harmful changes in aging brains
According to the authors, these findings suggest a possible physiological threshold beyond which severe heat exposure may become more harmful to the aging brain. However, the study did not directly measure the biological processes involved or establish a precise temperature threshold.
Preclinical experimental evidence in rats also shows a threshold for blood-brain barrier impairment at higher temperatures (38°C for four hours) compared to 35°C.
The authors offer plausible biological mechanisms, including reduced cerebral blood flow, neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, chronic cortisol elevation, and secondary effects such as poor sleep and dehydration. However, these were not demonstrated in the current study and remain hypotheses only.
The findings suggest that neighborhood infrastructure and cooling capacity may be associated with heat-related dementia risk beyond individual-level characteristics. However, the researchers measured estimated neighborhood AC prevalence rather than individual household AC ownership or use, and did not establish that air conditioning directly protects against dementia.
These findings do not agree completely with prior work, where heat-related cognitive effects were concentrated among people with lower education or income.
Survey-based dementia assessments limit certainty about heat associations
The findings should be interpreted with some caution. As an observational study, the research cannot establish whether extreme heat directly contributes to dementia.
The researchers estimated outdoor heat exposure at the neighborhood level, meaning they could not account for differences in how much heat individuals experienced or the temperatures inside their homes. Estimates of central AC prevalence were also based on 2016 data and applied across the entire study period. If access to AC increased over time, this approach may have overestimated cooling availability in earlier years, potentially weakening the observed association.
Another limitation was that dementia was identified through survey-based cognitive assessments rather than clinical diagnoses. The researchers also lacked information on dementia subtypes, making it impossible to determine whether the associations differed between Alzheimer's disease, vascular dementia, and other forms of the condition.
Other unmeasured factors, including environmental pollutants, diet, and genetic susceptibility, may have influenced the findings. Although the researchers could not completely rule out the possibility that people experiencing early cognitive decline had moved to hotter areas, additional analyses provided little evidence that such moves explained the results.
Finally, the study could not assess lifetime heat exposure, leaving questions about the longer-term effects of extreme heat on dementia risk.
Study highlights need for community-focused extreme heat adaptation
The authors conclude that outdoor heat-index conditions of 103°F or more, occurring even a few days each year over several years, may be associated with increased dementia risk. They suggest that dementia prevention strategies should consider local extreme heat exposure and prioritize approaches that may reduce cumulative thermal stress, particularly in disadvantaged communities.
In high-heat areas, the authors recommend moving beyond generic heat action plans designed for whole populations, toward locally appropriate strategies developed with residents. These could combine structural improvements, including reflective roofs and better-insulated housing, with affordable measures such as staying hydrated and limiting outdoor activity during extreme heat. They also recommend prioritizing resources for communities facing socioeconomic and infrastructure constraints.
-
Choi, E. Y., Mage, S. M., & Ailshire, J. A. (2026). Outdoor extreme heat-related dementia risk and the role of socioeconomic disparities: evidence from 20 years of data on US older adults. Alzheimer’s & Dementia. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1002/alz.71857. https://alz-journals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/alz.71857

Presidential family meetings are needed to manage the current heatwave
Mabila Mathebula|Published
Dr Mabila Mathebula is an author, ghostwriter, and life coach, and has a PhD in Construction Management.
Image: Supplied
Sea-surface temperatures in the Central and Eastern Pacific have surged to unprecedented levels. The warming of the globe is our current human challenge facing the entire world.
Should people be taken aback by the current rogue weather patterns whirling around the globe? I am certainly not surprised. Based on research conducted at the prestigious Stanford Research Institute (SRI) during the early 1970s, the ability to witness events from a distance has been called remote viewing.
Other viewers peering into our future in recent times report a great wave of fire and heat (Braden, 2000).
When I was in high school, our biology teacher took infinite pains to explain how radiant energy from the sun is converted into chemical potential energy; he called the whole process photosynthesis.
I was ignorant of the fact that the same sunny radiant energy has the potential to cause Malignant Melanoma (skin cancer). The current oppressive heatwave is now threatening the smooth running of our society. It is time that President Cyril Ramaphosa proactively held ‘Family Meetings’ with a view to guiding the nation to exercise enough caution.
If left unattended, Malignant Melanoma can spread rapidly to other parts of the body with fatal results. Skin cancer is directly linked to sunlight and ultraviolet (UV) light. Ultraviolet radiation still penetrates fabrics to some extent. In the four hours between 11:00 and 15:00, it is when two-thirds of the ultraviolet radiation of every day occurs.
Siesta should apply in Africa, not Europe. Dr Marianne Alexander once wrote, “Sunlight in South Africa is one of the most potentially dangerous in the world.”
The President is fully aware of the fact that South Africa adopted the Sendai Framework for Disaster Reduction 2015 -2030. This is a voluntary management agreement adopted in March 2015 by 187 United Nations members in Japan.
The framework states that, “While the enabling, guiding, and coordinating role of the national and federal State Government remain essential, it is necessary to empower local authorities and local communities to reduce disaster risk, including through resources, incentives and decision-making responsibilities, as appropriate.”
The people who are hard hit by the current oppressive heatwave are rural people who walk long distances to access basic services, as well as outdoor workers such as railway and construction workers, as much time is spent bending over. The back, particularly the shoulders, ears, and the neck, are the most exposed parts of the body and should be protected.
Some politicians are doing door-to-door campaigns under these hot conditions. Some are planning the rallies for the local government elections regardless of the weather. The government must come up with regulations to manage this heatwave – this is not micromanagement but responsible governance. This might also affect the schooling system as well.
People who organise mass gathering events such as marches, rallies and church events during this heatwave are always in the danger zone. This simply means that these events must also start early when the temperature is cool and end before people are exposed to the oppressive heatwave. Outdoor Sporting events also need leaders to be careful.
The current tug of war between the government and faith-based organisations also warrants our attention. For example, we have seen the Saudi Arabian government regulating the use of loudspeakers at the mosques in Mecca as well as the banning of preaching on public transport in Ghana. It is notable that there are still those denominations that worship under the trees and some worship in a shelterless environment as part of their church tradition. This is a hazard that needs to be managed solicitously.
The Motsepe Foundation has been at the forefront of the annual National Prayer Day (NPD) at the FNB Stadium, where different faith-based organisations intercede for the nation. I call down the love of God to bless and empower this nation with good weather during the NPD. I also call down the peace, joy, and power of God to bless and empower this nation during the NPD.
This brings me to the November 4 local government elections. The following questions keep flooding back: At what time must the voting stations open to protect the voters from the oppressive heatwave? At what time will the voting stations close? Will there be ambulances at the voting stations to transport people to hospital in case of emergency? Will the hospitals have the capacity to treat the heatwave patients?
The health authorities in South Africa have been sounding the C.A.R.E warning in good faith. Cover up, avoid the sun from 11:00 to 15:00, rub on sunscreen, and examine your skin regularly. Only a few people heeded this call.
We do not need to remove viewing, but common sense to manage this looming disaster proactively. We should take a leaf out of the book of the Titanic disaster. The Titanic disaster is recognised as an iconic example of human failures in transport technology and culture. Approximately 900 000 immigrants entered the United States of America between 1900 and 1914, and the Titanic was part of that economic shift.
Titanic captain EJ Smith had reached the zenith of his career and was due to retire at the end of the voyage. He had sailed this route in the Olympic, and he knew the hazards posed by ice in the North Atlantic.
Other ships sent several warnings of icebergs; some were sent to the bridge, but the result was a small course adjustment. A smaller shy Californian had stopped in the ice field nearby. Its crew saw distress rockets sent up by the Titanic in the distance. However, the captain did not grasp what they meant.
President Cyril Ramaphosa is our current captain. I suggest that the President, in conjunction with the private sector, must plan, implement, and manage programmes to raise awareness and limit exposure. The unintended consequences of failing to manage the current heatwave would be lost productivity, occupational diseases, strokes and cancer.
The adage that prevention is better than cure still holds water. There is always a huge price to pay for being stubbornly reactive, and there is a bonus for being a learning organisation.
Dr Mabila Mathebula is an author, ghostwriter, and life coach, and has a PhD in Construction Management.

The weather department has also issued warnings for thunderstorms, lightning and gusty winds for three days beginning October 28. Image for representational purpose only.
| Photo Credit: Biswaranjan Rout
Cyclone Arnab, which is expected to make landfall along the Andhra Pradesh coast on Wednesday (October 28, 2026), is set to bring heavy rainfall in parts of Jharkhand for three days, prompting the State government to ask district administrations to maintain vigil, officials said.

A 'yellow' alert (be updated) of heavy rain has been issued for Ranchi, Khunti, Simdega, Gumla, Lohardaga, Saraikela-Kharsawan, East and West Singhbhum for 24 hours starting from 8.30 a.m. on October 28, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) said.
The rain intensity is likely to increase thereafter, with IMD issuing an 'orange' alert (be prepared) for seven Jharkhand districts — Garhwa, Palamu, Latehar, Lohardaga, Gumla, Simdega and West Singhbhum — for 24 hours till 8.30 a.m. on October 30, according to a weather bulletin.
"A heavy rainfall alert has also been issued for Chatra, Koderma, Hazaribag, Ramgarh, Ranchi, Khunti, Saraikela-Kharsawan and East Singhbhum from 8.30 am on October 29 for 24 hours," it said.
The weather department has also issued warnings for thunderstorms, lightning and gusty winds for three days beginning Wednesday (October 28, 2026).
"The very severe cyclonic storm Arnab over west-central Bay of Bengal moved nearly westwards and lay centred at 5.30 am on Tuesday (October 27, 2026) over the same region. It is very likely to move west-northwestwards till evening of October 27," Ranchi Meteorological Centre Deputy Director Abhishek Anand said.
"The district administrations have been directed to remain vigilant and prepared to deal with adverse conditions," an official said.
The Ranchi district administration has asked its officials to be vigilant over the situation.
"Waterlogging is likely in low-lying areas and on roads in Ranchi due to heavy rainfall. Kutcha houses, shanties, and structurally weak buildings may sustain damage. Rivers, lakes and large drains could overflow. There is a possibility of flood-like conditions in low-lying areas," the administration said in a statement.
It is also anticipated that standing crops in fields could be damaged due to the accumulation of water, it added.
Keeping the possibilities in mind, Ranchi Deputy Commissioner Manjunath Bhajantri has issued instructions to all officials concerned to keep a constant watch on the situation and ensure necessary preparations.
Published - October 27, 2026 12:18 pm IST

Proposal has been made in Verkhovna Rada to allow businesses to operate without taking shelter during "yellow" alert, provided employees consent
Members of Parliament are proposing to allow businesses to operate during a yellow-level air raid alert without taking shelter, provided that employees consent.
This was announced by Ihor Fris, a member of parliament from the "Servant of the People" party, according to Censor.NET.
"We have just drafted and submitted for signature to our colleagues from all parliamentary factions and groups in the Verkhovna Rada a draft resolution of the Verkhovna Rada calling on the Cabinet of Ministers to amend the government resolution that requires businesses to ensure the availability of shelters during a yellow alert," the statement reads.
What does this entail?
The draft resolution proposes that businesses be allowed to operate without shelters if the employee consents.
It was previously reported that Ukrainian businesses must ensure the availability of shelters or safe spaces for employees and visitors by December 4, 2026. If they fail to comply with this requirement, they will not be able to continue operations when a yellow-level air threat is declared.
